lessons.title: Three parts of a story
lessons.outcome: Sequence a short drama with a group.
lessons.goal: I can put a short story in order with my group.
success: I can show the start, change and end.
I can use my part or cue.
I can keep my own choice in my arts log.
words: A sign to start or stop.
What comes first, next and last.
The part you do in a group.

artist_cards.work: The new den with still pictures
artist_cards.description: The group point at a big space. Next they show a small space with their hands. Last they point to a new small den. They hold each pose for three counts.
artist_cards.notice: What comes first? What comes last?
artist_cards.prompt: How can a still pose show the change?
artist_cards.model_answer: The big space comes first. The small den comes last. Wide hands then close hands show that the space has changed.

artist_cards.work: The new den with a voice cue
artist_cards.description: A voice says Start, Next, End. The group make one pose at each cue. In the middle a helper says, Can we change it? The group point to a new plan.
artist_cards.notice: Which word helps the group change pose?
artist_cards.prompt: Which cue could help our group?
artist_cards.model_answer: Next helps the group move to the middle pose. We could use the same short cue, or a silent hand cue.

staff_guidance.plain_language: Resilience can include pausing, asking for help, changing a plan and trying a manageable next step. It does not mean hiding feelings, tolerating harm or continuing through pain.
staff_guidance.scope: Both pathways work at Explore. Each lesson is complete without the optional GROW next level stretch. Keep records for the award; these lessons alone do not complete or certify it.
staff_guidance.art_specialist_help: Demonstrate a small clear pose and a calm cue rather than an expert performance. Look for a sequence, a purposeful choice, contribution and a confirmed reflection. Still, seated or pupil-directed performance is equally valid.
staff_guidance.sensory_and_emotional_access: Use invented situations. No personal accounts, surprise noise, touch, contact, shouting or forced eye contact. Offer seated movement, silent gesture, narrator or director roles. Pupils may share with a trusted adult only. Agree a calm place and a return cue before starting.
staff_guidance.safety: Check a clear personal space before any movement. Walk only; no running, lifting, falling, climbing, throwing or actual building. Keep all imagined props imaginary. Use an agreed open-hand stop cue. Do not move another pupil or their chair.
prompt_ladder: Point to the instruction or place.
Model the first step only, then return the task.

adaptations.cognition_and_learning: Show one story beat at a time. Rehearse three or four beats with concrete cue words. Model the first pose, then fade the adult lead. Check the pupil can point to the next beat.
adaptations.communication_and_interaction: Offer pointing, signing, a narrator line, directing or an adult scribe. Give processing time. Use I chose ... because ... and First ... next ... last ... .
adaptations.semh: Keep the event fictional and low stakes. Agree roles with pupils. Allow a pause, role change or private audience. Praise a specific contribution rather than confidence or compliance.
adaptations.sensory_and_physical: Perform from a chair, use hands only or direct an adult. Avoid unexpected sound and touch. Ensure personal space. A silent cue is valid.
adaptations.eal: Plan in any language. Pair story cues with gestures. Accept oral rehearsal or a labelled sketch. Check the intended story order rather than accent or spelling.

misconceptions.claim: A group drama needs everyone to speak.
misconceptions.correction: An actor, silent mover, narrator or director can make a real creative contribution. Record what each pupil actually decides and does.

misconceptions.claim: Resilience means the first plan must succeed.
misconceptions.correction: Show the character pause, ask for help or choose a new plan. A change of method can be the point of the story.

misconceptions.claim: A final group performance proves every pupil made each choice.
misconceptions.correction: Keep individual contributions and confirmed words alongside a group record. Record the help used and any unfinished part honestly.

staff_guidance.careers_line: Performers, directors and stage teams use cues, agree roles, rehearse safely and respond to feedback.

cold_call.middle: Which cue helps the next part start?
cold_call.higher: How does the last pose show the new plan has worked?

ta_focus.I do: Point to the matching story beat. Check the pupil can identify the change before asking for a reason.
ta_focus.We do: Invite one choice per pupil. Model the first step only and give the choice back. Agree an accessible role.
ta_focus.Independent: Record each pupil's actual decision or action and the support used. Use a short question before offering a choice. Do not count an adult model as pupil evidence.

lessons.artist_use_note: Both comparison cards are invented classroom examples. They are not real artists, recorded performances or evidence of an external arts encounter. Read or demonstrate them with calm gestures.
lessons.evidence: Retain a dated sequence sketch or cue record, a brief adult observation of the real performance or rehearsal, and each pupil's own confirmed arts-log words. Record the contribution, change and support actually used. A photograph or recording is optional under local consent procedures. Never enter a teacher model as pupil work.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Choose to act, speak, point or direct.
Keep a clear space. Stay in your own space.
This is a made-up story. You can sit.
stages.say: We will make a tiny story in three parts. You can be a mover, a voice or a director. You may sit and use your hands. We will not touch, run or build a real den. Show an open hand to stop.
stages.good: Each pupil confirms an accessible role and the stop cue. Adult checks clear space.
stages.fallback: Offer two roles: show a hand pose or tell the adult which pose to show.
stages.answer: A pupil may direct one pose while another pupil performs it. That is a valid role if the choice is the pupil's.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Our story is The new den.
Start: We want a den in a big space.
Change: The space is too small.
End: We choose a small den.
Point to the end.
stages.say: I will read three parts. Hold up one finger for the start, two for the change and three for the end. Which part shows the new plan? We can change a plan and still tell a good story.
stages.good: Pupils identify the ending as the small den and notice the space changes.
stages.fallback: Read only the start and end. Ask the pupil to point to the one that shows the new plan.
stages.answer: The small den is the end. The small space is the change. The group changes its plan rather than trying to force a big den into the space.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch three still poses.
One: Point at a big space.
Two: Hold hands close. Look and pause.
Three: Point at a small den.
Hold each pose for three slow counts.
stages.say: Watch me tell the story with hands only. First I point wide. Next I hold my hands close to show the space is small. I pause and say, Can we change it? Last I show a small roof with my hands. Now I mix up the order. Does the new plan still come last? Tell me which pose to move.
stages.good: The adult contrasts ordered and mixed beats. A pupil identifies or directs a correction. Check understanding before group practice.
stages.fallback: Use just three spoken cues and hand shapes at the desk. The pupil can hold up one, two or three fingers.
stages.answer: Start then change then end makes the new plan clear. If the small-den pose comes first, the audience may not see why the plan changes.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Pick a role in our group.
Choose a pose for each part.
Use Start, Next, End as cues.
Try all three in order.
Which pose shows the change?
stages.say: Let us use one idea from each person. A mover may show a pose, a voice may give a cue, and a director may choose the pose. With four pupils two can share a pose role. Everyone keeps their own space. Try our three parts. Can we see the small space before the new den?
stages.good: Each pupil offers or confirms a creative choice. Group holds three poses in order and uses an agreed cue.
stages.fallback: Adult reads the cues while pupils choose hand shapes. A pupil may direct the adult to show their chosen shape.
stages.answer: A close hand shape can show the small space. A small roof shape may show the new den. Other clear, safe choices are valid.

stages.name: Create
pupil: In your group, make three parts.
Choose your role and one idea.
Try the story twice.
Keep the order: start, change, end.
In your book or arts log, draw or tell your three parts.
Add: My choice was ___.
stages.say: For the first three minutes choose roles and poses. Rehearse for four minutes. For three minutes test a cue or change a pose so the story is clear. Use the last four minutes to keep a three-part sketch or adult-written record and your own choice. No actual den is built. Ask for a pause if you need one.
stages.good: Group performs or directs an ordered three-part story. Each pupil has an identifiable contribution and keeps an individual record.
stages.fallback: Use the supplied story exactly, with hand poses and an adult caller. The pupil chooses one pose or cue and confirms the three-part record.
stages.answer: Example only: I chose close hands for the change. Our start is wide space, our change is small space, and our end is a small den. A pupil may use their own safe ending if it follows the change.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Show the three parts to a partner or the adult.
The watcher says: I saw ___ first.
Did the new plan come last?
Choose one thing to keep.
Sit and put books away with care.
stages.say: The watcher describes the order, not how brave anyone was. Say I saw ... first, then ... . Maker, confirm or correct that account. Use the final two minutes to settle and store the sequence for tomorrow. No public performance is required.
stages.good: Audience identifies order and pupil confirms one choice to retain. Record honest uncertainty where the change was not clear.
stages.fallback: Adult watches one hand sequence privately and asks which pose the pupil wants to keep.
stages.answer: Useful feedback: I saw the wide space first and the small den last. A useful next step: hold the middle pose a little longer.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: My role was ___.
My choice was ___.
Our story went first ___, next ___, last ___.
Next time I will ___.
stages.say: I can write your words and read them back. Tell me if I have got your idea right. Keep your own choice, not my sample. Write or confirm today's date and the help you used.
stages.good: Dated log records individual contribution, sequence and a real next step.
stages.fallback: Pupil points to one of the three poses; adult records the confirmed choice and what the pupil directed.
stages.answer: Example only: My role was director. I chose the small roof. Next time I will hold the change pose longer.

Supported: Pick a role with the adult.
Try the three parts with help.
Tell or point to your own choice.
Independent: Agree your role and one idea.
Make the start, change and end.
Use one cue for each part.
Try twice and keep the order.
Keep your own choice in your arts log.
Aspire: Test a spoken cue and a silent cue.
Choose which helps the order most.
Say why and keep that choice.

misconceptions: A still pose cannot tell a story
Three clear poses in order can show a start, change and end.
Everyone must speak
A silent pose or a pupil-directed adult pose is a valid contribution.
The group must build a real den
All objects and places are imagined. Show the idea with safe gestures.
kit: For three or four pupils: books or arts logs and pencils.
A clear personal space for each pupil, or seats with safe room for hand gestures.
Three cue words read from the activity card: Start, Next, End. No real den, sticks, boxes or props.
Keep the three-part sequence and individual log ready for the next lesson. No camera or device is required.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Point wide. Say: We want a den. Hold for three counts.
15 to 30 seconds
Hands close. Pause. Say: The space is small.
30 to 45 seconds
Ask: Can we change it? Make a small roof with hands.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to the three parts. Say: Start, change, end. I kept that order.
models: Teacher model only: First we want a den. Next the space is small. Last we make a small den. I chose a small roof pose.
Teacher model only: I directed the change pose. I asked the mover to hold close hands for three counts.
lessons.cover: Read The new den from the Starter stage. Assign accessible roles without requiring speech. Model three hand poses, then let the group choose and rehearse three poses in order. Use Start, Next, End cues. Keep a dated three-part sketch or adult observation plus each pupil's own confirmed contribution. Keep the sequence for the next lesson.

success: I can show our story in order.
I can use a clear cue or pose.
I can say what we changed.
words: A sign to start or stop.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find our three-part story.
Choose your role again. You may change it.
Sit or stand in your own clear space.
Use the open-hand stop cue.
stages.say: Today we will make The new den clear for a watcher. You can keep your role or change it. A hand pose, cue or directing choice counts. If our record is missing, we will make the three parts again and date them today.
stages.good: Pupils retrieve or rebuild a truthful sequence and confirm roles and stop signal.
stages.fallback: Read the three story beats from today's Starter and offer hand poses or directing.
stages.answer: Missing work is not reconstructed as evidence from yesterday. A fresh attempt is recorded with today's date.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: First: We want a den.
Next: The space is small.
Last: We choose a small den.
Put these parts in order.
Point to the part we can make clearer.
stages.say: Tell or point to the first, next and last parts. Which part did our watcher find hard to see? If no one watched yet, the adult will watch one calm try now. Choose one part to improve.
stages.good: Pupil recalls the order and chooses a specific pose or cue for improvement.
stages.fallback: Adult shows two possible changes: hold the middle pose longer or use a Next cue. Pupil chooses.
stages.answer: The useful target is a clear change or cue, not louder speech or bigger movement.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch a fast change. It is hard to see.
Watch a slow cue and a still pose.
Which is clear?
I change one thing.
I keep the same story order.
stages.say: I rush from the big space to the small den. Now I hold close hands for three counts and wait for Next. The story has the same three parts. I changed the time I held the middle pose. Which try let you see the change?
stages.good: Adult isolates one change and models before and after. Pupil links hold time or cue clarity to story understanding.
stages.fallback: Use only hands at the desk. Count quietly or show three fingers without speaking.
stages.answer: A longer middle pose gives the watcher time to see the small space. A clear silent cue may be as useful as speech.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Agree one change to our group story.
Try it once.
A watcher points to the change.
Keep it or try again.
Use kind words: I saw ___.
stages.say: Choose one target as a group: cue or pose. We will try both versions calmly. Watcher, name a feature you saw. Maker, say whether it fits your idea. No one needs to act out a real worry.
stages.good: Group uses a cue and compares versions. Each pupil confirms a role or a creative decision.
stages.fallback: Adult calls cues while one pupil chooses how long to hold the middle pose. Let another pupil watch privately.
stages.answer: Example feedback: I could see the small space when the pose stayed still. A valid alternative: the silent cue helped us move together.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Rehearse your three-part story.
Change one cue or pose.
Show the story in order.
Share with a partner or the adult.
In your book or arts log, keep the change and your own part.
stages.say: Use four minutes to rehearse and three to test the one agreed change. Use three minutes to share with your chosen watcher, then four to log your own contribution and feedback. A pupil may direct an adult, narrate, move or give a silent cue. Do not stretch arms into another person's space.
stages.good: Ordered story is shared or privately demonstrated. Log captures individual contribution, before-and-after change and actual feedback.
stages.fallback: Use the original three hand poses and adult cues. Pupil changes one pose hold or points to the cue the adult should use.
stages.answer: Example only: Before we rushed the change. Now we hold close hands for three counts. My job was the Next cue. The watcher said the change was clear.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Watcher: What came first and last?
Maker: What did we change?
Say one thing to keep.
Thank the group.
Settle and store your log.
stages.say: Ask one watcher to describe the start and end. Each maker names or points to their own contribution. A quiet private share is enough. Spend the last two minutes settling, storing work and clearing the space.
stages.good: Watcher identifies order. Pupil describes or confirms a real change without claiming all group choices.
stages.fallback: Adult reads a short observation back to the pupil to confirm or correct.
stages.answer: Useful record: The pupil gave the Next cue after the change pose and chose to hold that pose longer. Record adult prompts separately.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: My role was ___.
We changed ___ to ___.
It helped because ___.
My next step is ___.
stages.say: Make a short honest record. If the story is still a rehearsal, say so. You can draw, point, speak or ask me to write your words. We will keep the work for the award.
stages.good: Dated pupil reflection links one changed feature to story clarity, with actual support recorded.
stages.fallback: Offer cue or pose as a choice, then record the pupil's confirmed reason or gesture.
stages.answer: Example only: We changed a fast pose to a slow still pose. It helped the watcher see the small space. My next step is to wait for the cue.

Supported: Choose cue or pose as your change.
Independent: Rehearse your group story.
Change one cue or pose.
Share with your chosen watcher.
Keep feedback and your own part.
Say how the change helped.
Aspire: Ask which makes the order clear.
Choose one and give a reason.

misconceptions: Improving a scene means making it louder
A clearer cue, pause or held pose can improve the story.
We must change the whole story
Change one feature so the audience can follow the same order.
A group record is enough for everyone
Each pupil confirms their own part and help used.
kit: For three or four pupils: books or arts logs and pencils.
A clear personal space for each pupil, or seats with safe room for hand gestures.
Three cue words read from the activity card: Start, Next, End. No real den, sticks, boxes or props.
Bring the previous sequence and logs if available. If missing or the pupil was absent, make a fresh attempt and date it today.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Rush the three hand poses once. Ask what was hard to see.
15 to 30 seconds
Repeat with a still close-hand middle pose. Hold for three counts.
30 to 45 seconds
Use a calm Next cue. Say: I changed one thing.
45 to 60 seconds
Say: The held pose made the small space clear. Keep the real choice and feedback.

Teacher model only: Our silent cue helped us move together. Next time I will wait until all are still.
lessons.cover: Retrieve the three-part den story or rebuild it from today's Starter. Model a rushed version and a calm version with a held middle pose. Let pupils choose one cue or pose to change. Rehearse, share with an agreed small audience and keep actual feedback plus each pupil's own log. No prior attendance, device or prop is required.

lessons.title: Devise a story about a new plan
lessons.outcome: Devise a short performance about overcoming change.
lessons.goal: I can help devise a short performance that shows a change and a new plan.
success: I can help order four story beats.
I can contribute a performance choice.
I can record my choice and a next step.
words: One small part of a drama.
A sign that tells a performer when to act.
Change a plan to fit a new need.

artist_cards.description: Four roles plan a show with wide arm moves. The imagined space becomes smaller. A planner asks the group for ideas. They rehearse small arm moves and finish together. A narrator names each change.
artist_cards.notice: Which action lets the audience see the problem?
artist_cards.prompt: Which detail shows how the group responds to change?
artist_cards.model_answer: Wide moves followed by small hand moves show the space becoming smaller. Asking for ideas and testing small moves show an active response.

artist_cards.description: The group begin with wide poses. A silent palm cue marks a smaller space. One performer pauses and looks at the group. Each offers a small move. They choose one and repeat it together, then hold the final pose.
artist_cards.notice: How does this group show a choice without speech?
artist_cards.prompt: How could we use a pause or repeated move in our own scene?
artist_cards.model_answer: Each performer offers a move. Repeating the chosen move together makes the choice visible. A pause could show thinking before a new plan.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Choose a role: mover, voice, narrator or director.
You can work seated or use silent gestures.
Keep your own clear space.
Our story is invented. You do not need a personal story.
stages.say: We will devise a short scene about a group that changes its plan. Agree a calm open-hand stop cue. Choose an acting, voice or directing role that fits you. No contact, running or loud sound is needed.
stages.good: Each pupil confirms a role and access route. Adult checks safe space and the stop cue.
stages.fallback: Offer a silent director role: the pupil chooses the cue or pose and an adult performs it.
stages.answer: A creative contribution can be a deliberate cue, a pose or a choice of order; it does not require public speech.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Story seed: A group plan a show in a wide space.
The space becomes smaller.
They pause, ask for ideas and change the moves.
They finish the show in the smaller space.
What changed? What did the group do?
stages.say: This is a made-up story called A smaller show space. Nothing really blocks our room. What is the change? Which choice helps the group respond? We will show a manageable change, not act out personal distress.
stages.good: Pupils separate the changed space from the group's response of pausing, asking and adapting.
stages.fallback: Use two prompts: What got smaller? What did they change? Offer hands wide then close as a visual cue.
stages.answer: The space got smaller. The group changed wide moves into small moves after asking for ideas. They did not need to force the old plan to work.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch two short examples.
One uses a narrator. One uses silent cues.
Find four beats: plan, change, choice, result.
Which feature makes the choice clear?
stages.say: Read or demonstrate both fictional comparison cards with calm hand movements. In one example I say, What could we try? In the other, I pause, invite a small hand move and repeat it. Which feature shows the group choosing a new plan? Check: does a wide first pose belong before or after the small-space cue?
stages.good: Pupil identifies four beats and compares narration with pause, invitation or repetition. Adult checks the story order before independent work.
stages.fallback: Read one card and show only two contrasting hand shapes. Ask the pupil to place the change before the new move.
stages.answer: The wide first pose goes before the small-space cue. Repeating a chosen small move can make the group's decision visible without words.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Build four beats as a group.
Plan: agree the first idea.
Change: show the smaller space.
Choice: ask for help or test a small move.
Result: show the new plan working.
Choose cues and roles.
stages.say: Each person offers one small idea or chooses one offered by a peer. With up to five pupils, use mover, narrator, director or cue roles; roles may be shared. Test a short four-beat version. Does the audience see what changed and what the group chose to do?
stages.good: Group creates a workable four-beat outline with agreed accessible roles and a clear response to change.
stages.fallback: Keep the supplied story and offer two choices at the choice beat: ask a helper or test a small move. Pupil selects and directs it.
stages.answer: A clear choice could be a narrator question followed by small moves, or a silent pause followed by offered hand moves and an agreed repeated one.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Devise a scene of about 30 to 60 seconds.
Keep the four beats in order.
Each person contributes a choice.
Try it twice. Test one cue, pause or move.
In your book or arts log, keep the outline and your part.
stages.say: Use three minutes for roles and the outline, five for two calm trials, two to decide what to keep, and four to log each person's contribution. Use the supplied story or a similar invented low-stakes change. If sound is chosen, use quiet original words or hand taps below speaking volume. Stop on the agreed cue.
stages.good: Real scene or directed scene has a clear change, response and result. Each pupil identifies an actual creative contribution and a trial.
stages.fallback: Use seated hand gestures and adult narration for the four beats. Pupil directs one beat and confirms the outline and reason.
stages.answer: Example only: I chose a pause before the small move so the audience could see the character thinking. Our group tested narration and silence, then kept the narrator.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Show a trial to a peer or the adult.
Watcher: What changed? What helped?
Maker: Confirm or correct that reading.
Choose one feature to improve next lesson.
Store the outline and settle.
stages.say: Give descriptive feedback using I noticed ... . The maker can correct the audience's reading. Agree one next step linked to clarity rather than confidence. Use the last two minutes to store outlines, clear the space and settle.
stages.good: Audience reads the change and response. Maker records a specific next step while retaining the first attempt.
stages.fallback: Adult watches privately and reads back a short exact observation for pupil confirmation.
stages.answer: Useful feedback: I saw the space shrink, but the new plan was rushed. Next step: hold the chosen small move before the final pose.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: My role and choice were ___.
Our four beats were ___.
We tested ___ and kept ___ because ___.
Next time I will ___.
stages.say: Keep your own words and the support used. An adult may write and read them back. Mark a trial as a trial. Do not copy a model reflection or claim another pupil's decision.
stages.good: Dated individual reflection explains an actual choice, trial and next step.
stages.fallback: Pupil points to a beat and confirms a choice; adult records the observed action and confirmed words.
stages.answer: Example only: I directed the pause at the choice beat. We kept a silent hand cue because it helped us start together. Next time I will make the final pose clearer.

Supported: Make one cue, pose or voice choice with help.
Tell or show your choice for the arts log.
Independent: Devise four clear beats as a group.
Agree roles and safe cues.
Try a scene of 30 to 60 seconds twice.
Keep one tested feature for a reason.
Record your own part and a next step.
Aspire: Complete the same scene and log.
Test two ways to show the choice beat.
Ask which helps the audience see the response.
Use the feedback to explain your choice.

log: The four beats are plan ___, change ___, choice ___, result ___.
My role was ___. My own choice was ___.
We tested ___ and ___. We kept ___ because ___.
misconceptions: Overcoming change means the character feels happy at once
A pause, a request for help or a workable new plan can show a response. The ending need not remove every feeling.
More speech makes the story clearer
A still pose, silent cue or repeated move may make a choice clearer.
The audience must guess the exact intended feeling
Ask what the audience saw, then let the maker explain their intention. More than one reading is possible.
kit: For up to five pupils: books or arts logs and pencils.
Clear personal spaces or seats for hand-gesture performance. All props and spaces in the story are imagined.
Read the two fictional performance cards aloud. Use an adult-written four-beat outline if needed.
No device, instrument, costume, scenery or external performance is needed. Retain the first outline and individual logs for the next lesson.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Show wide arms within your safe space. Say: Our first plan has wide moves.
15 to 30 seconds
Bring hands close. Say: The imagined space is smaller. Pause.
30 to 45 seconds
Ask: What could we try? Offer a small hand wave, then repeat it.
45 to 60 seconds
Hold a final small pose. Say: We changed the move. Our four beats show the new plan.
models: Teacher model only: My role was narrator. I asked What could we try? before the small moves. That helped the audience hear the group make a choice.
Teacher model only: We tested a spoken cue and a silent cue. I chose silence because the group watched the hand signal together.
lessons.cover: Read the smaller-space story and both fictional comparison cards. Model plan, change, choice and result with safe hand movements. Pupils devise a short scene using accessible roles and original words or silent movement. Compare two trials and keep a four-beat outline, observation and individual arts-log contributions. Keep this attempt for the next lesson.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Compare the two fictional examples. Choose a skill for your own role, such as cue timing or clear narration. Describe a starting point, practise once and note what changes.
stretch.evidence: Keep the comparison, personal skill goal, first trial and a dated reflection in your arts log. Use your own words or confirmed dictated words.
stretch.why_optional: This may support later next level review. It is optional and does not change today's Explore success criteria or complete the award.
stretch.good: Pupil makes a feature-based comparison and links a chosen skill to an observed change in their own role.
stretch.fallback: Adult records the pupil's comparison and watches a short directed trial. The pupil confirms what changed.

lessons.title: Refine and share a story about change
lessons.outcome: Devise a short performance about overcoming change.
lessons.goal: I can refine and share our devised performance using feedback.
success: I can keep a clear change and response in our scene.
I can improve one performance feature.
I can record feedback and my own contribution.
words: Practise a scene before sharing it.
A comment that helps you review your work.
The move from one story beat to the next.

artist_cards.description: Four roles plan a show with wide arm moves. The imagined space becomes smaller. A planner asks the group for ideas. They rehearse small arm moves and finish together. A narrator names each change.
artist_cards.notice: Which action lets the audience see the problem?
artist_cards.prompt: Which detail shows how the group responds to change?
artist_cards.model_answer: Wide moves followed by small hand moves show the space becoming smaller. Asking for ideas and testing small moves show an active response.

artist_cards.description: The group begin with wide poses. A silent palm cue marks a smaller space. One performer pauses and looks at the group. Each offers a small move. They choose one and repeat it together, then hold the final pose.
artist_cards.notice: How does this group show a choice without speech?
artist_cards.prompt: How could we use a pause or repeated move in our own scene?
artist_cards.model_answer: Each performer offers a move. Repeating the chosen move together makes the choice visible. A pause could show thinking before a new plan.

staff_guidance.plain_language: Resilience can include pausing, asking for help, changing a plan and trying a manageable next step. It does not mean hiding feelings, tolerating harm or continuing through pain.
staff_guidance.scope: Both pathways work at Explore. Each lesson is complete without the optional GROW next level stretch. Keep records for the award; these lessons alone do not complete or certify it.
staff_guidance.art_specialist_help: Demonstrate a small clear pose and a calm cue rather than an expert performance. Look for a sequence, a purposeful choice, contribution and a confirmed reflection. Still, seated or pupil-directed performance is equally valid.
staff_guidance.sensory_and_emotional_access: Use invented situations. No personal accounts, surprise noise, touch, contact, shouting or forced eye contact. Offer seated movement, silent gesture, narrator or director roles. Pupils may share with a trusted adult only. Agree a calm place and a return cue before starting.
staff_guidance.safety: Check a clear personal space before any movement. Walk only; no running, lifting, falling, climbing, throwing or actual building. Keep all imagined props imaginary. Use an agreed open-hand stop cue. Do not move another pupil or their chair.
prompt_ladder: Point to the instruction or place.
Model the first step only, then return the task.

adaptations.cognition_and_learning: Show one story beat at a time. Rehearse three or four beats with concrete cue words. Model the first pose, then fade the adult lead. Check the pupil can point to the next beat.
adaptations.communication_and_interaction: Offer pointing, signing, a narrator line, directing or an adult scribe. Give processing time. Use I chose ... because ... and First ... next ... last ... .
adaptations.semh: Keep the event fictional and low stakes. Agree roles with pupils. Allow a pause, role change or private audience. Praise a specific contribution rather than confidence or compliance.
adaptations.sensory_and_physical: Perform from a chair, use hands only or direct an adult. Avoid unexpected sound and touch. Ensure personal space. A silent cue is valid.
adaptations.eal: Plan in any language. Pair story cues with gestures. Accept oral rehearsal or a labelled sketch. Check the intended story order rather than accent or spelling.

misconceptions.claim: A group drama needs everyone to speak.
misconceptions.correction: An actor, silent mover, narrator or director can make a real creative contribution. Record what each pupil actually decides and does.

misconceptions.claim: Resilience means the first plan must succeed.
misconceptions.correction: Show the character pause, ask for help or choose a new plan. A change of method can be the point of the story.

misconceptions.claim: A final group performance proves every pupil made each choice.
misconceptions.correction: Keep individual contributions and confirmed words alongside a group record. Record the help used and any unfinished part honestly.

staff_guidance.careers_line: Performers, directors and stage teams use cues, agree roles, rehearse safely and respond to feedback.

cold_call.middle: Which cue helps the next part start?
cold_call.higher: How does the last pose show the new plan has worked?

ta_focus.I do: Point to the matching story beat. Check the pupil can identify the change before asking for a reason.
ta_focus.We do: Invite one choice per pupil. Model the first step only and give the choice back. Agree an accessible role.
ta_focus.Independent: Record each pupil's actual decision or action and the support used. Use a short question before offering a choice. Do not count an adult model as pupil evidence.

lessons.artist_use_note: Both comparison cards are invented classroom examples. They are not real artists, recorded performances or evidence of an external arts encounter. Read or demonstrate them with calm gestures.
lessons.evidence: Retain a dated sequence sketch or cue record, a brief adult observation of the real performance or rehearsal, and each pupil's own confirmed arts-log words. Record the contribution, change and support actually used. A photograph or recording is optional under local consent procedures. Never enter a teacher model as pupil work.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your outline and last next step.
Choose your role and audience.
Use seated, silent or directed performance if needed.
Keep clear space and the open-hand stop cue.
stages.say: We will improve one part of our invented scene. Choose a peer, small group or trusted adult as audience. If work is missing or you were absent, use the four-beat story and make a fresh version today. Do not add an earlier date to new evidence.
stages.good: Pupil retrieves a genuine starting point or begins a fresh dated attempt and confirms an accessible role.
stages.fallback: Read the four beats from the Starter and let the pupil choose one to direct.
stages.answer: A fresh attempt is valid. It must not be described as a performance that happened in the previous lesson.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Recall four beats: plan, change, choice, result.
Which beat shows the response to change?
Read the real feedback from our trial.
Pick one target: cue, pause, voice or move.
stages.say: In our story the space gets smaller. The response is the group asking for ideas and trying small moves. What did our watcher actually notice? If we have no feedback yet, I will watch a brief trial now and describe one thing I see. Choose one useful target.
stages.good: Pupil distinguishes event from response and chooses one target grounded in a genuine observation.
stages.fallback: Offer two visible targets: hold the choice pose longer or give a clear silent cue.
stages.answer: The change is smaller space. The response is the new plan. A target should help the audience see that link.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch the choice beat rush past.
Now watch a pause, a cue and a small move.
What is clearer?
I keep the story. I change one feature.
I check what the watcher saw.
stages.say: First I rush through the new idea. Now I pause, ask What could we try? and repeat a small move once. For this test I am changing the pause length only. Tell me if that gives the audience time to see the choice. A later test could change the cue, but we will not change everything at once.
stages.good: Adult models controlled refinement and an audience check. Pupil links the tested feature to clarity.
stages.fallback: Use one hand gesture and a counted silent pause. Pupil chooses the shorter or longer pause.
stages.answer: Holding a pause can mark thinking and separate the change from the new plan. A shorter pause may be preferred if the group can still make the choice clear.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Agree our one target.
Try the scene once.
The watcher names what they see.
Choose whether to keep the change.
Confirm roles and cues for sharing.
stages.say: Use one kind specific comment: I could see ... when ... . Makers, decide whether to keep the tested change. Feedback informs your choice; it does not take the choice away from you. Make sure every pupil has a real creative contribution and knows the stop cue.
stages.good: Group tests one feature and makes an evidence-based decision. Watcher comment is precise and maker confirms the choice.
stages.fallback: Adult watches a seated trial and gives one concrete observation; pupil chooses keep or change.
stages.answer: Example: I could see the decision when you held the offered move before copying it. The group might keep that hold because it makes agreement visible.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Rehearse the scene with the agreed change.
Keep plan, change, choice and result.
Share for about 30 to 60 seconds.
Ask: What changed? What helped the group?
In your book or arts log, keep your role, feedback and next step.
stages.say: Use five minutes to rehearse and three to share with the chosen small audience. Use two minutes for the audience questions and four for individual logs. A private directed demonstration is valid. Watchers describe features and keep comments kind. Keep sound below speaking level and all movement within each person's own space.
stages.good: Short performance or directed scene clearly shows a change and response. Each pupil retains an individual account of their contribution, real feedback and a next step.
stages.fallback: Use four seated hand poses and adult narration. The pupil directs the improved cue or pause, and a trusted adult watches privately.
stages.answer: Example only: I changed the cue from a spoken Next to a held hand. The watcher saw us start the new move together. I will keep that cue and next work on a clear final pose.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Audience: Name the change and the new plan.
Makers: Explain one choice you made.
Say what helped the audience follow the story.
Thank the audience.
Store work and settle.
stages.say: Ask each maker to confirm their own part. If the audience missed a beat, keep that as useful feedback rather than pretending it worked. No rating of confidence or personal disclosure is needed. Use the last two minutes for calm storage and clearing the space.
stages.good: Reflection compares intention and audience reading honestly, including an unfinished feature if relevant.
stages.fallback: Adult reads back a brief observation and asks pupil to confirm or correct the own-contribution record.
stages.answer: Useful reflection: The audience saw the smaller space but missed the request for help. Our next step is to hold the choice beat longer.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: My own role and choice were ___.
We changed ___ because ___.
The watcher noticed ___.
This helped or did not yet help because ___.
My next step is ___.
stages.say: Date the log and record actual support. Keep the first attempt and this later version if possible. Your arts log can show useful change even when the scene is still in rehearsal. This is evidence towards the award, not a claim that all its requirements are complete.
stages.good: Dated reflection records a specific before-and-after feature, real feedback and an honest next step.
stages.fallback: Pupil points to the changed beat and confirms an adult-written record. Record what was observed, not an inferred feeling.
stages.answer: Example only: I directed a longer pause. The watcher saw the new plan clearly. Next I will practise giving the final cue without an adult prompt.

Supported: Use the four-beat story and an adult cue.
Try it and share privately if you wish.
Confirm the feedback and your next step.
Independent: Use real feedback to choose one target.
Rehearse and keep the four beats.
Share with your chosen audience.
Check what the audience understood.
Record your contribution and next step.
Aspire: Complete the same share and reflection.
Compare your first and later versions.
Explain which feature changed the audience reading.
Set a clear skill goal for your own role.

log: My role and own choice were ___.
Our first version had ___. Our later version had ___.
The change helped or did not yet help because ___.
misconceptions: We must accept every suggestion
Listen, test and choose what fits the intended story. Explain the decision.
Sharing means performing to a whole class
A chosen peer or trusted adult can be the audience. A directed or seated scene is valid.
Feedback must say the performance was perfect
Honest specific feedback supports a useful next step. Record what actually happened.
kit: For up to five pupils: books or arts logs and pencils.
Clear personal spaces or seats for hand-gesture performance. All props and spaces in the story are imagined.
Read the two fictional performance cards aloud. Use an adult-written four-beat outline if needed.
Bring previous outlines and genuine trial feedback if available. If absent or missing, create a fresh trial today. Keep individual contribution records separate from the group outline.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Show a rushed choice beat with small hand moves.
15 to 30 seconds
Repeat with a held pause before the same hand move.
30 to 45 seconds
Ask the watcher what became clearer. Keep their actual comment.
45 to 60 seconds
Say: I changed the pause. It helped the choice stand out. My next step is a clear end cue.
models: Teacher model only: I was the cue keeper. I held my hand cue until all were ready. The watcher saw the new move start together.
Teacher model only: We kept our story but made the choice beat longer. The audience still missed the final result, so that is our next step.
lessons.cover: Retrieve the four-beat smaller-space scene or make a fresh dated trial from the Starter. Choose one target using actual feedback. Model testing one feature. Rehearse, share with an agreed small audience, ask what changed and what helped, then record actual feedback and each pupil's own contribution. No audience beyond a trusted adult, prior work or device is required.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Compare your plan with what the viewer saw. Which part showed the change best? Use a real detail. Say why you will keep or change one part. Plan a way to check your next skill goal.
stretch.evidence: Keep your plan, your own part and real feedback. Add your choice and reason. Add a skill goal and a way to check it.
stretch.why_optional: This may support later next level review. It is optional, adds no requirement to today's Explore task, and does not itself complete the award.
stretch.good: Pupil links a skill change to evidence from trials, considers the audience reading and sets a specific manageable next step.
stretch.fallback: Adult asks what changed and reads back the pupil's own words. Pupil confirms one next practice action.

scope: Explore for both pathways. Optional GROW next level stretch retains additional evidence without changing core success criteria.
timing: Arrival 0-3; Starter 3-6; I do 6-12; We do 12-18; Create 18-32; Review 32-37; Exit 37-40 minutes.
